That's a fair comparison. I personally like the kitchen metaphor. The Chef is the CPU, some work faster and some work slower, sometimes you have more than one. RAM is like counter space, how much stuff can be placed into 'working memory' isn't all worked on at once, but the access time to that counter space is -much- faster than access time to the fridge or pantry. Fridge/pantry/whathaveyou is a HDD.

On a traditional desktop, you have a cpu and ram for day to day tasks, input output, fetching files, etc.
You would also have a separate gpu to process nothing but graphical output to a monitor. It's still a processor, just optimized for different tasks that are required for generating an image on a display.
VRAM is the memory that is dedicated specifically to that graphics processor. In a new gaming rig, you'll see gigabytes of VRAM alongside the powerful GPU on a video card.
On 'integrated' graphics that is often used for mobile devices, there isn't really a separate processor or memory, it's like teaching the CPU to do different work to process the graphics. That means that for 'vram' you are either allocating a set ammount of 'counter space' just for graphics files, or varying that ammount depending on the load.

The big strain from games is the number of different things that are interracting with one another in a virtual space. That space is chock-full of mesh models that represent characters and model their interractions with one another. Then you have the textures that need to be wrapped around the mesh frames to make the character look a certain way. Graphics 'quality' can be a number of things. It could be the number of background objects (foliage, particle effects, etc) It can be the ammount of detail in the mesh model (A good example of a low-quality mesh is FF7) Or it could be the resolution (image size) of the texture image that is added to the model to add small details.
All of these things make the files larger, and require more counter space plus a faster chef to pick up the extra things in the same timeframe.

If you're using a mod for tons of extra characters on-screen at once, then you need more VRAM to handle all of it at once, and a super fast GPU to actually process them all in a timely fashion so you don't get lag, or characters popping in and out of existance.
Graphics quality is dependant on higher VRAM and a little faster GPU to load the bigger texture file, but it's really just a different image being used.
Extra vram could keep things on-screen longer, but bodies disapearing in a generic shooter is usually just a timer, not a lack of resources. Although, they could lower the timer for lower graphics settings to help out a little.

First of all, the whole "GHz = thinking" is not actually all that accurate. This is referred to as the clock speed, and it basically relates to how quickly parts of the CPU can communicate with each other. Every time the clock "ticks," everything in the chip moves ahead one step It needs to be synchronized because if it isn't, then nothing is coordinated and the communications get garbled; you could have part of the CPU trying to add two numbers another part supplied it, but one of those numbers is no longer useful and the other number is being recalculated so it comes through in chunks or nonsense.

However, what can often be far more important is how well the CPU's innards are laid out. For instance, modern CPUs try to predict what it's going to do next. If you've got a piece of crummy prediction circuitry that's super simple, then you have fewer parts to coordinate so you can ramp up the clock speed. However, a "smarter" chip with complicated prediction circuitry may be able to predict instructions much better, so even if its clock speed is slower, it may be able to get more work done in the same time because it's not screwing up the predictions.. So unfortunately there is no one single measurement of how "good" a computer is; it's just too complicated. That said, it is accurate that, in most cases, the higher clock speed (GHz) will usually be a better system, though there are enough exceptions that it's worth noting that this is not always the case.

Now, on to your general questions.

A GPU is basically an auxilliary processor for your computer. The CPU is a very powerful processor, but its abilities are limited. While it can do anything a GPU can do, it is burdened by the fact that it is a general purpose processor and thus must be able to do just about anything a Turing machine can do (a Turing machine being the theoretical model on which computers are based). A GPU does not have the same requirement; much of the thinking is going to be done for it by the CPU. As such, it can devote a huge amount of the space and parts on board into doing specific types of calculations insanely quickly. It is also able to have lots and lots of processing parts so that it can have many different parts doing the exact same job at the same time. This is called parallel processing. While parallel processing is not always helpful, a modern, 3D-oriented video game is one situation where additional parallel processing will almost always be of some benefit. A better GPU will have not only a better clock speed (in general), but it will also have more pipelines (chains of components that work on instructions like an assembly line) and more sophisticated parts. In short, a GPU does specific types of math that are especially useful for 3D graphics, and the more math the chip can do, the better experience you have in play.

What RAM does varies greatly depending on precisely what you're doing with it. The most blatantly obvious is keeping information from going into the swap file. A modern computer does not usually "run out of memory" the way that one would think it does. Rather, when a task takes up too much memory, it puts some of it on the hard disk. A hard disk is on the order of hundreds of thousands to millions of times slower (or more) than an electrical circuit, so while this allows you to do a task that requires more RAM than your machine physically has, it also means it will do that task very slowly. More RAM means more of this information is kept out of the swap file. It also helps in other ways. For instance, lt's say that you have different graphic modes. You can have simplistic (crummy, but functional) graphics or you can have extremely complicated (good but slow) graphics. In this case, if you don't have enough RAM then you're going to be reloading that information from the disk more often because more complicated graphics usually require more RAM - often a lot more - than simple graphics. As such, you get a better play experience because the computer can hold more of what it's processing in a much quicker component. It is worth noting that the GPU's RAM will often be where a lot of the graphical information is kept, e.g. more complicated textures, for a number of reasons that amount to "it's much, much faster."

Now, as for your specific questions:

If you're playing a mod with more men, ALL THREE will help you. A faster CPU will be able to let it keep track of more men in general, and keep everything going more readily and without lag. A faster GPU will allow those men to be drawn more quickly, and with more detail. And RAM will allow it to hold all of those men together without having to hit the hard disk as often, and will help with other tasks, such as storing more complicated graphical information. Corpses fading out may be helped by more RAM, although precisely how this is done is going to vary from game to game, since the game program is responsible for keeping track of if, and when, and how, corpses (and just about anything else) will disappear.
